name: The Great Cycad of Ryuge-ji

location.address: Ryuge-ji Temple, 2085 Muramatsu, Shimizu-ku, Shizuoka City, Shizuoka Prefecture

access: Paid entry to Ryuge-ji Temple grounds, reported around 400 yen adult / 200 yen child (aggregator source, not the temple's own site), viewing hours approximately 8:30-16:30
transport: JR Tokaido Line to Shimizu Station, then Shizutetsu Justline bus toward Shimizu City Hospital / Chureito, about 20 min, alight at the Ryuge-ji stop; or 20 min by car from the Tomei Expressway Shimizu interchange
story:
From the temple path this looks like a thicket of small palms. It is one plant, and fifty-eight thick trunks fan out of a single base 5.2 metres around.

A sago palm is not a palm. It is a cycad, from a lineage that was already ancient when the first flowering plants appeared, and it grows so slowly that all of this stands under four metres tall. Japan made it a Natural Monument on 9 December 1924, one of the first seven cycads in the country to be designated, and the botanist Honda Masaji called it the largest cultivated cycad in Japan. It is counted among the three great cycads, alongside one at Noman-ji and one in Sakai. It is a male specimen, which the 1924 register already recorded.

Its age belongs to the temple rather than to science. The placard says the plant was carried from China and given to Ryuge-ji by Tokugawa Yorinobu and Tokugawa Yorifusa, and puts it at roughly 1,100 years. No dating anybody can check has ever been published, so read that figure as the tradition it is.

What has been measured is the shape of it: 2.6 metres round on the north branch, 2.3 in the centre, 1.7 on the south, with the whole crown covering about nine metres in each direction. The temple charges a few hundred yen and the grounds are open roughly 8:30 to 16:30.

name: Kosugi no Osugi (the Totoro Tree)

location.address: 108-5 Magarikawa, Sakegawa Village, Mogami District, Yamagata Prefecture

access: Free, a village-designated natural monument with a public car park and marked path; Japanese Wikipedia notes the path from the car park to the tree is not snow-cleared in winter, implying open, unstaffed access the rest of the year
transport: No direct train or bus found; nearest station is JR Shinjo (Ou Main Line / Yamagata Shinkansen terminus), about 30 minutes by car or taxi from there. This is NOT within an easy transit reach of Tsuruoka, roughly 23km away in a straight line with no direct route found in the sources checked; access guidance in every source found points to Shinjo, not Tsuruoka
story:
People arrive at this cedar carrying umbrellas, so they can stand underneath and recreate a scene from an animated film. From the field below, the tree's two rounded crowns read as a pair of ears, and from about 2020 that resemblance turned a cedar in a village of northern Yamagata into a destination people fly in for.

The village had always read the same shape differently. The trunk divides into two cores just above the base, so the tree has long been Meoto-sugi, the married-couple cedar, and Enmusubi no Sugi, the matchmaking cedar. A mountain deity is enshrined at its foot. One local story has a lord of Shinjo, out hunting deer, sheltering under it from a blizzard.

The age is genuinely disputed. Japanese Wikipedia gives 700 to over 800 years. Yamagata Prefecture's own landscape register heads the entry with an estimate of 1,000. Neither states a method, so the honest answer is somewhere between seven hundred and a thousand years and nobody has narrowed it. The dimensions are firmer: 6.3 metres around the base, about 20 metres tall, a crown roughly 17 metres across.

Sakegawa Village listed it as a natural monument in November 1986. It is free, with a car park and a marked path, about half an hour by car from Shinjo station and no closer by train. The path is not cleared in winter, and this part of Yamagata gets a great deal of snow.
